e96ebd4f07.q: How can leaders separate facts from stories they tell themselves in high-pressure situations?
e96ebd4f07.a: You take the client back to a micro moment to see what the facts are versus their perspective or story. For example, when a boss says 'step into my office,' that is the neutral reality—those are just the facts with no interpretation. Your story about it is your perspective, and you have a choice about which one you believe. By separating these two, leaders can see what they can actually take back control over, because your brain immediately interprets situations unconsciously, creating an entire experience before the actual conversation happens.

ab00ec2fd2.q: What is the growth model that Modern Leadership uses to help leaders change their behavior patterns?
ab00ec2fd2.a: The growth model gets clients to see that when they think a particular story or perspective, they show up in a specific way—usually not showing up well for the other person and also not showing up well for themselves, which is called beating yourself up internally. The coaching job is to show somebody that their brain thinks automatically along this path, then ask if they want to start choosing to think something different so they can create something different. Almost every time, clients say yes and want to explore what else they could think.

a735318525.q: How should leaders respond when they are called into their boss's office to avoid creating negative narratives?
a735318525.a: Rather than assuming negative outcomes, frame it as: no matter what happens, you will learn, grow, and become stronger for it, and while you are in there, you will show the type of leader you are—you will not overreact or yell, and you will take whatever feedback is given and learn from it. This reframe allows you to walk through the door differently, and when you receive feedback calmly and ask what the definition of done looks like next time, your boss is more likely to respond positively than if you had gone in with defensiveness or self-doubt.

4c6603fb08.q: Why does blaming others prevent leaders from growing and taking control of their results?
4c6603fb08.a: If you blame others for what happened, you give away all your power to them—if it is always someone else's fault, you cannot change the situation and you are powerless to do better. But if you acknowledge what you could have changed, even though it feels scary because it feels like failure, it means you are actually in control of whether your results can be better next time. This is why taking ownership is essential for growth.
